---
title: $\LaTeX$ for Stat230
format: html
---

$\LaTeX$ is a language for writing math. If you plan to take a lot of math/stat courses, it is incredibly useful to be able to write out nice looking mathematical equations. 

This is a bare-bones introduction to latex meant to help you for the type of equations we'll use a lot in Stat230. 

# Math mode in Quarto

Since our activities, homework, and quizzes are all `.qmd` files, you don't need a full standalone LaTeX document, you just need to know how to turn on "math mode" inside a regular Quarto file. There are two ways to do this:

**Inline math** for a symbol or short expression in the middle of a sentence. Wrap your equation in single dollar signs: `$\beta_1$` renders as $\beta_1$.

**Display math** for an equation that should get its own centered line. Wrap your equation in double dollar signs:

```
$$
\hat{y}_i = 3.4 + 2.3 x_i
$$
```

renders as

$$
\hat{y}_i = 3.4 + 2.3 x_i
$$

A few habits that will save you time:

::: callout-tip
Every `$` needs a matching `$` (and every `$$` needs a matching `$$`). A missing dollar sign is the #1 reason a Quarto document fails to render. If you get a cryptic LaTeX error when you render, check that your dollar signs are paired first.
:::

::: callout-tip
Underscores (`_`) and carets (`^`) only mean "subscript" and "superscript" *inside* math mode. If you type `beta_1` outside of `$...$`, Quarto will try to interpret the underscore as markdown formatting (italics) instead of a subscript, and it won't look right.
:::

# Basic building blocks

| Code | Renders as | Used for |
|----|----|----|
| `x_1` | $x_1$ | subscripts |
| `x^2` | $x^2$ | superscripts (exponents) |
| `\hat{y}` | $\hat{y}$ | a "hat" (predicted/fitted value) |
| `\bar{x}` | $\bar{x}$ | a "bar" (sample mean) |
| `\beta_0`, `\beta_1` | $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ | population regression coefficients |
| `\varepsilon_i` | $\varepsilon_i$ | the error term |
| `\hat{\beta}_1` or `b_1` | $\hat{\beta}_1$ or $b_1$ | an estimated (fitted) coefficient |
| `\frac{a}{b}` | $\frac{a}{b}$ | a fraction |
| `\sqrt{x}` | $\sqrt{x}$ | a square root |
| `\log{x}` | $\log{x}$ | natural log |
| `\sum_{i=1}^{n}` | $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$ | a sum |
| `\times` or `\cdot` | $\times$ or $\cdot$ | multiplication (don't use a plain `*`) |
| `\leq`, `\geq`, `\neq` | $\leq$, $\geq$, $\neq$ | $\leq$, $\geq$, $\neq$ |
| `\sim` | $\sim$ | "is distributed as" |
| `\overset{iid}{\sim}` | $\overset{iid}{\sim}$ | "is independently and identically distributed as" |
| `\pm` | $\pm$ | plus-or-minus (handy for confidence intervals) |
| `\text{words}` | $\text{words}$ | regular (non-italic) text *inside* math mode |
| `\left(`, `\right)` | $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)$ | brackets that auto-resize around tall content like fractions |

# Writing out regression models

Here's how the notation you'll be asked to reproduce all term actually looks in Quarto source.

**The theoretical SLR model:**

```
$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)
$$
```

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

**The fitted SLR model**:

```
$\hat{y}_i = 2.3 + 3.2 x_i$
```

**A hypothesis test**, written in symbols:

```
$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ vs. $H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0$
```

$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ vs. $H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0$

**A confidence interval**, showing the general form and a filled-in example:

```
$$
b_1 \pm t^* \cdot SE(b_1)
$$

$$
0.519 \pm 1.656 \times 0.0345
$$
```

**The MLR model**, once you have more than one predictor (note the second subscript on $x$, indexing *which* predictor):

```
$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i
$$
```

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i
$$

**A model with a transformed response**: keep the transformation *outside* the $Y_i$ on the left:

```
$\log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$
```

**Logistic regression** uses the same right-hand side, but on the log-odds (logit) scale:

```
$$
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i
$$
```

$$
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i
$$

Notice the `\left(` and `\right)` around the fraction. Without them, the parentheses print at a fixed small size and look cramped around a tall `\frac{}{}`. Compare `(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})`  $(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})$  to `\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)` $\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)$.

# Common mistakes

::: callout-tip
**Forgetting the dollar signs.** `beta_1` in regular text just prints as "beta_1". You need `$\beta_1$` to get $\beta_1$.
:::

::: callout-tip
**Using `*` for multiplication.** `2 * x` inside math mode renders with an odd-looking asterisk. Use `\times` ($\times$) or `\cdot` ($\cdot$) instead, or just put the terms next to each other (`2x` renders as $2x$).
:::

::: callout-tip
**Mixing words into math mode without `\text{}`.** `$Y_i if x_i > 0$` tries to italicize and squish together "ifxi0" as if it were all variables. Wrap the words: `$Y_i \text{ if } x_i > 0$` renders as $Y_i \text{ if } x_i > 0$.
:::

::: callout-tip
**Copy-pasting from Word or a PDF.** Just like with regular text in your `.qmd` files, don't paste formatted equations in from another program. Retype them using the syntax above, or you'll get rendering errors that are hard to track down.
:::

# Quick reference

| Code | Renders as |
|----|----|
| `$\beta_0$`, `$\beta_1$` | $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ |
| `$b_0$`, `$b_1$` | $b_0$, $b_1$ |
| `$\hat{y}_i$` | $\hat{y}_i$ |
| `$\bar{x}$` | $\bar{x}$ |
| `$\varepsilon_i$` | $\varepsilon_i$ |
| `$\overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$` | $\overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$ |
| `$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$` | $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ |
| `$H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0$` | $H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0$ |
| `$b_1 \pm t^* \cdot SE(b_1)$` | $b_1 \pm t^* \cdot SE(b_1)$ |
| `$R^2$` | $R^2$ |
| `$\log(Y_i)$` | $\log(Y_i)$ |
| `$\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)$` | $\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)$ |
